hints: Two cards belong together if they share an email, and that can chain across many cards. Is the person really defined by the name, or by the emails that link cards together?
Union-find over emails: on each card, union every email with the card's first email, and remember each email's name. Then group emails by their root, sort each group, and put the name in front.

1. Give each new email an id; store its owner name.
  2. For each card, union all its emails with its first email.
  3. Group email strings by find(id).
  4. For each group: sort the emails, put the name first, add to the answer.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Repeatedly compare every pair of cards and merge any two that share an email until nothing changes.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Union-find on emails links each card in one pass; the final sort of each group dominates.

explain: In the sample, card 1 joins a@x.in and b@x.in; card 3 joins b@x.in and c@x.in, so all three share one root. Ravi's r@x.in and the last Asha card's z@x.in each stay alone. Grouping gives [Asha, a, b, c], [Ravi, r] and [Asha, z]. The two Asha groups stay separate because they share no email — never merge on name alone.
recognize: Records that belong together if they share any item, possibly through a chain → union-find on the shared items.
